config.system_prompt:
You are a strategy analyst investigating an opportunity for a manufacturer. Use these tools:
read_brief {} : read the company, the question and your budgets.
frame_problem {"objective":"...","constraints":["..."],"alternatives":["..."]} : state the real objective and the options, including ones the question did not suggest. Accepted once.
search_evidence {"query":"..."} : keyword search of the evidence. Uses one search.
challenge_theory {"theory_id":"T1","query":"..."} : search for evidence that could prove a theory wrong. Uses one search.
read_source {"id":"..."} : read a result found by search.
add_theory {"claim":"...","who_benefits":"...","why_behaviour_changes":"...","how_value_is_captured":"...","assumptions":["..."],"predictions":["..."]} : add one causal theory of value. Returns its id.
assess_evidence {"theory_id":"T1","evidence_id":"...","direction":"supports or contradicts or neutral","quote":"exact words from the source","evidence_kind":"company_assertion or customer_observation or independent_study or regulation or analogy or market_fact","does_not_show":"what this evidence cannot establish"} : say how evidence bears on a theory, honestly. Use neutral if it does neither.
propose_test {"name":"...","theories":["T1","T2"],"method":"...","sample":"...","measure":"...","prediction_by_theory":{"T1":"...","T2":"..."},"decision_rule":"...","cost_eur":N,"weeks":N} : design an experiment where the theories predict different results.
revise_theory {"theory_id":"T1","status":"kept or revised or rejected","reason":"...","new_claim":"the changed claim, or none","evidence_ids":["..."]} : update a theory after new evidence.
finish {"recommendation":"...","target_customer":"...","value_proposition":"...","favoured_theory":"T1","next_action":"...","uncertainty":"...","would_change_if":["..."],"evidence_ids":["..."]} : end the investigation.

Reply with one JSON object: {"name": "<tool>", "arguments": {...}}. A user turn that starts with "Tool result:" is the output of your call. End by calling finish.

Work like a scientist, not a consultant.
1. read_brief, then frame_problem. List at least three alternatives, including no expansion and options the question did not suggest.
2. Search before you theorise. Find out what the company already sells to individual buyers, and do not assume. Read at least three sources.
3. add_theory at least twice, and a third time if you have a different cause. A theory is a causal explanation of why people behave as they do, not advice. Do not write "the company should". Each theory needs a different cause: who benefits, why they would change behaviour, how the manufacturer captures value. Give assumptions, and predictions someone could measure.
For example, from eyewear: "People treat glasses as a medical necessity. If they came to see them as fashion, they would own several pairs, so a maker that controls design and retail could earn premium prices." A rival theory would name a different cause.
4. assess_evidence for every theory, quoting the source's exact words. Say what kind of evidence it is and what it cannot show. A company's own claim is not proof of demand. Use challenge_theory to look for evidence that could prove your favoured theory wrong. If you find nothing against it, say so. Never force a contradiction.
5. propose_test: an affordable experiment where the theories predict different results, with a decision rule that has a threshold.
6. If new evidence arrives, read it and use revise_theory.
7. finish. Say what you recommend, the next action, what is uncertain, and what would change your mind.

Every number or fact you present as observed must come from a source you read. Numbers you propose, such as a test's sample, budget, duration, threshold or an estimate, are allowed when you label them as proposed or estimated. Your theories are hypotheses, not facts. Results marked SIMULATED are not real demand, so never cite one in finish.

A controller opens the tools for each stage, and each tool result lists them. Before you finish you will also use:
decline_test {"reason":"..."} : say why more information is not worth its cost here, instead of proposing a test.
state_position {"favoured_theory":"T1","recommendation":"...","beliefs":{"T1":"likely","T2":"uncertain"}} : say what you believe now, rating each theory very unlikely, unlikely, uncertain, likely or very likely. finish then also takes "beliefs".
A SIMULATED result is a what-if exercise. Reason as if it were real, and say what it would mean for your theories. A result can change nothing. Still keep it out of the evidence you cite.

Keep the professional-only core, and run the proposed 12-week test (X1) of institutional and trigger-linked channels for CPR kit completion before any investment decision. frame.objective: Decide whether Laerdal Medical should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for one specific use case (for example, bystander CPR training for individuals), beyond its professional resuscitation and simulation products, and identify what evidence would justify it.
constraints: Outside analyst, public sources only; no company contact or internal figures
Test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions
Existing reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be established from sources
Financial and contractual detail may not be public
Simulated results are not evidence and will not be cited
alternatives: A: No expansion, keep the professional-only focus on manikins and simulation for healthcare and training organisations
B: Consumer product sold direct to individuals, such as a home or public CPR training app, kit or subscription, possibly with a redesigned low-cost bystander manikin
C: Channel change, selling existing products to individuals through retail, e-commerce or pharmacy without redesign
D: Customer-group change, targeting schools, workplaces, sports clubs or public-access bodies (B2B2C) instead of individuals
E: Adjacent use case, linking training to in-home medical devices or telehealth refresher training
F: Partnership or licensing, where a consumer first-aid brand or app developer carries the individual channel and Laerdal supplies content or hardware

T1.claim: Individuals will not buy bystander CPR training for themselves at a price that covers a direct consumer channel, but institutions (hospitals, schools, employers) will fund kits for individuals, so value is captured by selling through those institutional intermediaries (B2B2C).
T1.who_benefits: Hospitals, employers, schools and charities that want to show community or family readiness, plus Laerdal if it sells kits in volume through them.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: A kit given at a moment of need (for example, discharge from neonatal intensive care) or as part of a programme removes the price and the decision to buy, so families train who would never have paid.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal sells kits or content in bulk to institutional buyers who distribute them free or subsidised, rather than selling retail to individuals.
assumptions: Institutions have budgets for community or family CPR training
Individuals complete training when it is given to them free
Laerdal's existing sales force and distribution can reach these buyers
predictions: Institutional kit programmes grow in number across regions
Uptake is high when kits are given at discharge and low when sold retail
Sales are concentrated in a few large buyers rather than many individuals
T1.first_claim: Individuals will not buy bystander CPR training for themselves at a price that covers a direct consumer channel, but institutions (hospitals, schools, employers) will fund kits for individuals, so value is captured by selling through those institutional intermediaries (B2B2C).

T2.claim: Individuals do not value CPR skill enough to pay for training themselves, and the purchase is driven by a trigger event (a family member's cardiac arrest, a new baby, a job requirement), so a consumer product only sells when it is tied to a moment of need and the value is captured through the trigger, not by general marketing.
T2.who_benefits: Families of high-risk patients, new parents, and people facing a specific risk or requirement, plus any seller able to reach them at the trigger point, such as hospitals, insurers or employers.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Generic CPR training is abstract and easy to postpone; a concrete event makes the skill feel urgent and personal, so people act when the trigger occurs.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal sells the kit at or near the trigger, through partners who meet people at that moment, instead of marketing to a broad consumer base.
assumptions: Trigger events are identifiable and reachable by a partner
Urgency drives completion more than price
Buyers at the trigger will pay or be funded
predictions: Completion rates are higher for trigger-linked kits than for general sales
General retail sales of CPR kits stay low relative to trigger-linked sales
Sales cluster around identifiable events such as NICU discharge or workplace requirements
T2.first_claim: Individuals do not value CPR skill enough to pay for training themselves, and the purchase is driven by a trigger event (a family member's cardiac arrest, a new baby, a job requirement), so a consumer product only sells when it is tied to a moment of need and the value is captured through the trigger, not by general marketing.

assessments.quote: received a donation of 500 Infant CPR Anytime kits from the American Heart Association (AHA), funded by the Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield Foundation. The kits contain tools to help new parents learn the lifesaving skills of infant CPR and infant choking relief in as little as 20 minutes and are being distributed to families being discharged from the ICN.
assessments.does_not_show: It does not show that Laerdal made or sold these kits, since the donor was the AHA with foundation funding. It shows nothing about purchase price, uptake rate, or whether individuals would pay for kits themselves. One hospital in one state is a single case.

assessments.quote: The kit is portable, making it easy to share with family members or close friends – resulting in more people trained.
assessments.does_not_show: It is the company's own marketing claim. It does not show that individuals buy the kit, that a trigger event drives purchase, or what price buyers pay. It does not show the number of people trained. It is neutral on whether generic buyers would pay without a trigger.

assessments.quote: RevivR is our free, interactive, online CPR training course. In just 15 minutes, you can learn how to save a life and receive your very own CPR certificate. It couldn't be simpler – you just need your mobile phone or tablet and a cushion to practice on.
assessments.does_not_show: This is a charity's own description of a free course, not a sales or uptake figure. It does not show how many people complete it, whether it displaces paid kits, or anything about institutional purchasing. It contradicts only the implied need for a paid individual product: a free alternative exists, so T1's value capture through selling kits faces competition. It does not contradict the institutional channel itself.

X1.name: Trigger versus channel test of CPR kit completion
X1.method: Three arms, each run for 12 weeks through partners. Arm 1: kit offered free through a trigger-point partner (for example, a maternity or NICU discharge team), with the partner handing it out at the event. Arm 2: same kit offered free through a general institutional channel with no trigger (for example, an employer mass email with a link). Arm 3: same kit sold at a paid retail or online price. All arms use the same kit and the same completion measure. Proposed budget is an estimate: partner fees and fulfilment, with the analyst assumption of 20000 EUR total.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 150 kit recipients per arm (450 total), drawn from partners willing to participate in a single region. Figures are proposed, not observed.
X1.measure: Proportion of recipients who complete a self-reported CPR practice session with the kit within 4 weeks, confirmed by an in-app or kit log. Secondary: time to completion.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Institutional free distribution (Arm 2) completes at a rate close to Arm 1, both well above paid retail (Arm 3). The institutional channel, not the trigger, drives completion.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Trigger-linked distribution (Arm 1) completes well above both Arm 2 and Arm 3. A free kit with no trigger (Arm 2) does little better than paid retail, so the trigger, not the channel, drives completion.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if Arm 2 completion is within 10 percentage points of Arm 1 and both exceed Arm 3 by at least 20 points, favour T1. If Arm 1 exceeds Arm 2 by at least 20 points and Arm 2 is within 10 points of Arm 3, favour T2. If neither pattern holds, keep both theories and do not invest further.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a new consumer proposition yet. Keep the professional-only core and run the proposed 12-week channel test (X1, proposed budget 20000 EUR, an analyst assumption) before any investment decision. Laerdal already has a home-oriented kit (CPR Anytime) sold or distributed beyond hospitals, so the question is whether the institutional route, not a broad consumer product, is where the value sits.
final.target_customer: Institutions that give CPR kits to families or staff at a trigger point (for example, neonatal intensive care discharge, workplaces, schools), not general individual consumers.
final.value_proposition: A CPR kit delivered free or subsidised by an institution at a moment of need, with completion tracked. Value to Laerdal comes from institutional volume. This is a hypothesis, not a demonstrated offer.
final.next_action: Confirm from public or partner sources whether Laerdal already sells CPR Anytime kits to institutions and at what scale, then run test X1 with a trigger-point partner, a non-trigger institutional channel and a paid retail arm.
final.uncertainty: High. I found no public sales, pricing, margin or contract data for Laerdal's individual-buyer or institutional kit business. The only verified observation linking kits to an institution is one hospital donation funded by the AHA and a foundation, not Laerdal. The free BHF RevivR course is a competitor-like alternative whose uptake I could not measure. Both T1 and T2 are supported only by the same single case and a company's own marketing claim, so both remain uncertain.
would_change_if: Public or partner data show Laerdal's individual kit sales are already large and profitable through retail, which would weaken the case for an institutional-only route.
Test X1 shows free non-trigger institutional distribution (Arm 2) completes far below trigger-linked distribution (Arm 1), which would favour T2 and a trigger-point partnership model.
Test X1 shows paid retail (Arm 3) completing at a rate close to the free arms, which would suggest individuals will pay and a direct consumer product could work.
Evidence that free alternatives such as the BHF course capture most demand, which would argue against any paid kit.
Evidence that institutions lack budget for CPR kits, which would weaken T1's value capture.

tool_result.title: CPR Anytime - Laerdal Medical
tool_result.excerpt: CPR Anytime is a flexible program that allows you to learn CPR at your own pace, in the comfort and privacy of your home. The kits can also facilitate large CPR training programs in school, workplace, or community settings. The kit is portable, making it easy to share with family members or close friends – resulting in more people trained.

tool_result.title: Dartmouth Health Children’s distributes infant CPR home training kits for families of babies treated in intensive care nursery
tool_result.excerpt: LEBANON – The intensive care nursery (ICN) at Children’s Hospital at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center (CHaD), New Hampshire’s only children’s hospital, recently received a donation of 500 Infant CPR Anytime kits from the American Heart Association (AHA), funded by the Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield Foundation. The kits contain tools to help new parents learn the lifesaving skills of infant CPR and infant choking relief in as little as 20 minutes and are being distributed to families being discharged from the ICN.
